items.title: Jobs on numbered workers
items.question: `k` workers are numbered 0 to `k - 1`. `jobs[i] = [arrive, length]`, and no two jobs arrive at the same time. Jobs are handled in order of arrival, though the list may come in any order. A job takes the free worker with the lowest number. If none is free, it waits in line for the next worker to come free. On a tie it takes the lower number. It then starts and runs for its full length. A worker that frees at time `t` can take a job that arrives at `t`. Write `busiest_worker(k, jobs)`, which returns `[busiest, last_end]`. `busiest` is the worker that ran the most jobs, the lowest number on a tie. `last_end` is the time the last job ends. With no jobs it returns `[0, 0]`. There may be 2,000 workers and 100,000 jobs.

widget.how: There are 13 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The last three use 100,000 jobs, two of them with 2,000 workers.
widget.solution:
import heapq

def busiest_worker(k, jobs):
    free = list(range(k))
    busy = []
    count = [0] * k
    last = 0
    for arrive, length in sorted(jobs):
        while busy and busy[0][0] <= arrive:
            heapq.heappush(free, heapq.heappop(busy)[1])
        if free:
            w, start = heapq.heappop(free), arrive
        else:
            start, w = heapq.heappop(busy)
        end = start + length
        heapq.heappush(busy, (end, w))
        count[w] += 1
        last = max(last, end)
    if not jobs:
        return [0, 0]
    best = min(range(k), key=lambda w: (-count[w], w))
    return [best, last]

feedback.correct: All the tests pass, including 100,000 jobs on 2,000 workers.
feedback.generic: A hidden test failed. Check a worker that frees as a job arrives, a job that waits, and the large cases.

explain.text: Keep two heaps: free workers by number, and busy workers by finish time, then number. Before each job, free every finished worker, or else take the earliest finisher. Each job then costs $O(\log k)$, where a scan of all workers costs $O(k)$ and stops on the large tests.

items.title: The cheapest route with one free link
items.question: Sites are numbered 0 to `n - 1`. `links[i] = [u, v, cost]` is a one-way link from site `u` to site `v`. Each `cost` is a whole number, 0 or more. You hold one voucher, which makes one link of your route free. Write `cheapest_with_voucher(n, links)`. It returns the least total cost from site 0 to site `n - 1`, or -1 if no route exists. There may be 20,000 sites and 100,000 links.

feedback.correct: All the tests pass, including the 100,000 links.
feedback.generic: A hidden test failed. Check a route that is dear before the voucher, one-way links, and a site that cannot be reached.

explain.text: Run Dijkstra on pairs (site, voucher used or not), so each site has two best costs. A link costs its price, or nothing if the voucher is unused; that step lands in the used copy. Spending the voucher on the cheapest plain route can lose to a dearer route made cheap.

items.title: One share a day, with a cap
items.question: `prices[t]` is the price of one share on day `t`. Each day you may buy one share, sell one share, or do nothing. You may never hold more than `cap` shares, or fewer than 0. You start with no shares and must end with none. Cash may go below zero along the way. Write `best_cash(prices, cap)` in C++. It returns the most cash you can end with. There may be 200,000 days, prices up to 1,000,000 and a `cap` up to 100.

explain.text: Keep the best cash for each holding from 0 to `cap`, and update it once a day. Holding $h$ comes from holding $h$, from $h - 1$ and a buy, or from $h + 1$ and a sale. That is $O(n \cdot \text{cap})$ work, and the totals need a `long long`.
